waitingPeriod.note: days:0 is right (no post-filing wait), but both statutory pinpoints in the description are wrong, and the reconciliation duty is mischaracterized as mandatory. s.1 contains the petition right and sole ground; s.2(3) says the court shall not grant a divorce unless satisfied on all the evidence that the marriage has broken down beyond reconciliation - it says nothing about conciliation referral. Reconciliation is s.8 ('Promotion of Reconciliation') and is discretionary: s.8(1) obliges the petitioner to inform the court of reconciliation efforts; s.8(2) says the court MAY adjourn and MAY direct a conciliation attempt if a reasonable possibility of reconciliation appears. The two-year bar is s.9, not s.1, and s.9(2) leave is granted on 'substantial hardship suffered by the petitioner or depravity on the part of the respondent' - not 'exceptional circumstances of exceptional hardship or exceptional depravity' (that is the Kenyan/English formula). The separate twoYearBar key repeats both errors.
waitingPeriod.correct: No mandatory waiting period after filing. The petitioner must inform the court of all reconciliation efforts (MCA s.8(1)), and the court MAY adjourn proceedings to attempt reconciliation where a reasonable possibility appears (s.8(2)) - referral is discretionary, not mandatory. No petition may be presented within two years of the date of the marriage (MCA s.9(1)), except by leave of court on the ground of substantial hardship suffered by the petitioner or depravity on the part of the respondent (s.9(2)).

court.note: MCA s.43: 'court' means (subject to section 40) the High Court or a Circuit Court. The template's 'HIGH COURT OF JUSTICE, [CITY]' names a court that genuinely hears divorce and matches Ghanaian caption practice; Circuit Courts have concurrent jurisdiction and the Chief Justice may transfer undefended actions to a District Court (s.40). Caption 'IN THE MATTER OF THE MATRIMONIAL CAUSES ACT 1971 (ACT 367)' is standard.

terminology.note: Petition / Petitioner / Respondent / 'Suit No.' are all correct. But the decree structure is fabricated: metadata decreeProcess claims 'Decree Nisi -> Decree Absolute' stages, effectiveDateRule says the marriage is not dissolved until the Decree Absolute, certificateNote references the Decree Absolute, and the template docstring says 'Process: Petition -> Reconciliation -> Hearing -> Decree Nisi -> Decree Absolute'. Act 367 abolished the nisi/absolute structure: s.37 ('Decrees to be Final') provides that every decree of divorce shall take effect from the date on which the court gave judgment. No provision of Act 367 creates a decree nisi.
terminology.correct: Under MCA 1971 s.37 a decree of divorce is final and takes effect from the date the court gives judgment. There is no Decree Nisi / Decree Absolute stage in Ghana; the court grants a single decree of dissolution.

grounds.note: The five facts listed are individually accurate and correctly lettered against s.2(1): (a) adultery + intolerability, (b) unreasonable behaviour, (c) desertion 2 years, (d) 2-year separation + consent (with the 'consent shall not be unreasonably withheld' proviso, correctly reproduced), (e) 5-year separation. But s.2(1) enumerates SIX facts, and both metadata and template omit fact (f): 'that the parties to the marriage have, after diligent effort, been unable to reconcile their differences' - a distinctive Ghanaian no-fault fact. The template docstring wrongly says the sole ground is 'proved by one of five facts'. Also, the sole ground (marriage broken down beyond reconciliation) sits in s.1(2); s.2 is the proof provision.
grounds.correct: MCA s.1(2): the sole ground for divorce is that the marriage has broken down beyond reconciliation, shown under s.2(1) by one or more of SIX facts: (a) adultery + intolerability; (b) unreasonable behaviour; (c) desertion for 2 years; (d) 2-year separation with consent (consent not to be unreasonably withheld); (e) 5-year separation; (f) that the parties have, after diligent effort, been unable to reconcile their differences.

residency.note: Marriage Act 2014 s.65 is the grounds provision for dissolution of a CHRISTIAN marriage (Part III) - adultery, cruelty, desertion 3 years, exceptional depravity, irretrievable breakdown. It contains no residency rule, and no section of the Act imposes a 'resident in Kenya at the time of filing' requirement. The only residence language in Part X is s.67 (recognition of FOREIGN decrees, referencing ordinary residence in Kenya for two years). The bottom-line practical point (no minimum durational residency) is true, but the stated rule and its pinpoint are invented.
residency.correct: The Marriage Act 2014 contains no express residency requirement for divorce petitions. Jurisdiction follows the Act's definition of 'court' (s.2: a resident magistrate's court), and petitions are in practice filed at the magistrates' court station where the parties reside; s.67 governs recognition of foreign divorce decrees.

waitingPeriod.note: days:0 is fine, and the Decree Nisi -> Decree Absolute description matches current practice (courts still issue a decree nisi made absolute after ~30 days to six weeks, though the Act itself is silent - see MTM v SNM [2024] KEHC 8241, noting the Marriage Act does not provide for a decree nisi but it is prudent practice: https://new.kenyalaw.org/akn/ke/judgment/kehc/2024/8241/eng@2024-07-10). The error: 'Mandatory reconciliation attempt required before the court proceeds (Marriage Act, 2014, s.67-68)'. s.67 is recognition of foreign divorces. The conciliation provisions are s.64 (Christian marriages - parties MAY seek church reconciliation bodies), s.66(4) (civil marriages - the court MAY refer a dispute to a conciliatory process agreed between the parties) and s.68 (customary marriages - parties MAY undergo conciliation/customary dispute resolution). None imposes a blanket mandatory court referral.
waitingPeriod.correct: No statutory waiting period. Conciliation under the Marriage Act 2014 is voluntary/discretionary and marriage-type specific: s.64 (Christian, optional church reconciliation), s.66(4) (civil, court may refer to a conciliatory process agreed between the parties), s.68 (customary, parties may undergo customary dispute resolution). In practice courts issue a Decree Nisi made absolute after roughly 30 days to six weeks, a practice inherited from the repealed Matrimonial Causes Act rather than required by the 2014 Act.

court.note: The template caption defaults to 'HIGH COURT OF KENYA AT [LOCATION]' and metadata assigns civil/Christian/customary/Hindu divorces to 'High Court - Family Division'. But s.2 of the Marriage Act 2014 defines 'court' as a resident magistrate's court, and divorce causes are filed and heard in the magistrates' courts (e.g. EWN v SCM, Divorce Cause E1007 of 2022, [2024] KEMC 9, decided in a magistrate's court: https://kenyalaw.org/akn/ke/judgment/kemc/2024/9/eng@2024-05-02). The Kadhi's Court attribution for Islamic marriages (Constitution Art. 170) is correct. The High Court hears appeals, not first-instance Marriage Act petitions.

Islamic marriages: the Kadhi's Court (Art. 170). The High Court hears appeals.

grounds.note: Two paragraph letters of s.66(2) are swapped in both metadata and template: the Act reads (a) adultery, (b) cruelty, (c) EXCEPTIONAL DEPRAVITY, (d) DESERTION for at least three years, (e) irretrievable breakdown - the files cite desertion as s.66(2)(c) and depravity as s.66(2)(d). The overarchingRequirement claiming 'for all grounds, the court must be satisfied the marriage has broken down irretrievably (s.66(1))' is doubly wrong: s.66(1) was the three-year bar (declared unconstitutional in National Assembly of Kenya v Kina & another [2022] KECA 548), and unlike Ghana/England the Kenyan Act has no overarching sole-ground provision - irretrievable breakdown is simply one ground, s.66(2)(e), particularised by s.66(6). The s.66(6) summary is also incomplete: the statute lists adultery; cruelty; willful neglect for at least two years; separation for at least two years (voluntary or by decree); desertion for at least three years; imprisonment for life or seven years or more; incurable insanity certified by two doctors; and any other ground the court deems appropriate. Finally, the grounds list is presented as universal when grounds are marriage-type specific: s.65 (Christian), s.66 (civil), s.69 (customary, incl. any valid customary-law ground), s.70 (Hindu, incl. conversion, rape/sodomy/bestiality), s.71 (Islamic law governs).
grounds.correct: s.66(2) civil-marriage grounds: (a) adultery; (b) cruelty; (c) exceptional depravity; (d) desertion for at least three years; (e) irretrievable breakdown. There is no overarching breakdown requirement; s.66(6) deems irretrievable breakdown on eight limbs (adultery; cruelty; willful neglect 2+ years; separation 2+ years; desertion 3+ years; imprisonment for life or 7+ years; certified incurable insanity; any other ground the court deems appropriate). Christian marriages use s.65, customary s.69, Hindu s.70, Islamic s.71.

waitingPeriod.note: No statutory waiting period or interim decree exists in SA law; the decree of divorce is a single final order effective when granted. The metadata correctly adds the s.6(1) safeguard: a decree shall not be granted until the court is satisfied with the provisions made for any minor or dependent child (and has considered the Family Advocate's report where an enquiry was instituted under the Mediation in Certain Divorce Matters Act 24 of 1987).

court.note: Template names 'HIGH COURT OF SOUTH AFRICA ([DIVISION])' with 'Case No.' assigned by the Registrar - a correct forum and caption style. The current s.1 definition of 'court' is any High Court (s.166 of the Constitution) or a court for a regional division under s.29(1B) of the Magistrates' Courts Act 1944 (divorce jurisdiction conferred by the Jurisdiction of Regional Courts Amendment Act 31 of 2008, effective 9 August 2010). So the Regional Divisions of the Magistrates' Courts are the common lower-cost alternative venue, but the High Court default is legally valid. The old special Divorce Courts were absorbed into the regional courts.

terminology.note: SA divorce is an action commenced by summons (Divorce Act s.1(2): an action is instituted on the date the summons is issued): the template's Combined Summons + Particulars of Claim with Plaintiff/Defendant labels, 'In the matter between' caption, WHEREFORE prayer, 'costs of suit' and 'further and/or alternative relief' all match SA High Court practice, and the metadata terminology (care and contact, primary care, maintenance) tracks the Children's Act 38 of 2005 vocabulary. grounds.note: The statutory pinpoints are right (s.3 limits decrees to two grounds; s.4(1) irretrievable breakdown, correctly paraphrased in the template's getGroundsText; s.5 mental illness (2-year non-discharge under a Mental Health Act reception order + two psychiatrists) and continuous unconsciousness (6 months + two medical practitioners incl. a neurologist/neurosurgeon), matching the metadata's 2-year/6-month figures). Two legal-reality errors remain: (1) the metadata classifies 'Mental Illness or Continuous Unconsciousness' under 'fault' - SA divorce law is entirely no-fault; s.5 is a no-fault ground; (2) the irretrievable-breakdown description says 'there are no specific enumerated facts required' and lists 'continuous unconsciousness' among the factors the court may consider - but s.4(2) DOES enumerate (non-exhaustive) evidentiary facts: (a) no cohabitation as husband and wife for a continuous period of at least one year, (b) adultery which the plaintiff finds irreconcilable with a continued marriage relationship, (c) the defendant declared an habitual criminal and undergoing imprisonment; and continuous unconsciousness belongs to s.5(2), not s.4.
grounds.correct: Both statutory grounds are no-fault: s.4 irretrievable breakdown - with s.4(2) expressly listing one year's separation, adultery + irreconcilability, and habitual-criminal imprisonment as facts the court may accept as proof (without excluding other evidence) - and s.5 mental illness or continuous unconsciousness. Continuous unconsciousness is a s.5(2) ground, not a s.4 breakdown factor.

residency.note: Metadata description and template getJurisdictionStatement both cite 'Matrimonial Causes Act 1973, s.5(2)' for the domicile/1-year-habitual-residence rule. MCA 1973 s.5 was 'Refusal of decree in five year separation cases on ground of grave hardship' and was REPEALED on 6 April 2022 by the DDSA 2020 (verified at https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1973/18/section/5). Divorce jurisdiction is s.5(2) of the DOMICILE AND MATRIMONIAL PROCEEDINGS Act 1973, as amended post-Brexit by SI 2019/519, which lists seven grounds: both parties habitually resident in E&W; both last habitually resident and one still resides; respondent habitually resident; (joint applications) either applicant habitually resident; applicant habitually resident for 1 year; applicant domiciled and habitually resident for 6 months; either party domiciled. The substance of the claim (domicile of either party, or 1-year habitual residence) is a workable conservative simplification (the 1-year rule strictly attaches to the applicant), but the Act cited is flatly the wrong statute, and it appears in the rendered jurisdiction statement of the filed document.
residency.correct: Jurisdiction is governed by the Domicile and Matrimonial Proceedings Act 1973, s.5(2) (as amended by the Jurisdiction and Judgments (Family) (Amendment etc.) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019): the court has jurisdiction if, among other grounds, either party is domiciled in England and Wales, or the applicant has been habitually resident there for at least one year ending with the application date (six months if also domiciled), or the respondent is habitually resident there. Matrimonial Causes Act 1973 s.5 is a repealed hardship provision and has nothing to do with jurisdiction.

residency.note: Metadata and template getJurisdictionStatement claim jurisdiction from 'domicile OR habitual residence in Scotland for at least 40 days (DMPA 1973, s.7)'. That conflates two different rules and understates the habitual-residence ground by a factor of nine. DMPA 1973 s.7(2A) (Court of Session, verified at https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1973/45/section/7) and s.8(2)(a) (sheriff court) require either party to be DOMICILED in Scotland on the date the action is begun OR HABITUALLY RESIDENT IN SCOTLAND THROUGHOUT THE PERIOD OF ONE YEAR ending with that date. The 40-day rule is s.8(2)(b): an additional sheriff-court venue requirement that either party was resident in the SHERIFFDOM for 40 days ending with that date (or for 40+ days ending not more than 40 days before, with no known Scottish residence). A person with only 40 days' residence in Scotland who is neither domiciled there nor 1-year habitually resident does NOT give the Scottish courts jurisdiction. Also, s.7 is the Court of Session provision; sheriff court jurisdiction (which this template invokes) is s.8.
residency.correct: Sheriff court divorce jurisdiction (DMPA 1973, s.8(2)): (a) either party is domiciled in Scotland on the date the action is begun or was habitually resident in Scotland throughout the one year ending with that date, AND (b) either party was resident in the sheriffdom for 40 days ending with that date (or resident there at least 40 days ending not more than 40 days before that date with no known Scottish residence). Court of Session jurisdiction: DMPA 1973 s.7(2A) (domicile or one year's habitual residence).

waitingPeriod.note: Correct: Scotland has no statutory post-filing or post-decree waiting period; the only time conditions are the separation periods built into the grounds (1 year with consent under s.1(2)(d), 2 years without under s.1(2)(e)), and the fault facts (adultery, behaviour) have no separation requirement. The decree of divorce is final when granted (no nisi/absolute two-stage), subject only to the 14-day appeal window before an extract decree is issued (scotcourts guide: https://www.scotcourts.gov.uk/taking-action/divorce-and-dissolution-of-civil-partnership/guide-to-divorce-and-dissolution-of-civil-partnership/).

Article 3 of the Order is the grounds provision, not the jurisdiction provision.

grounds.note: Four of the five facts are exactly right, with correct pinpoints: Art.3(2)(b) behaviour, Art.3(2)(c) desertion for 2 years, Art.3(2)(d) 2 years' separation with the respondent's consent, Art.3(2)(e) 5 years' separation. waitingPeriod.note: Days=0 is right — there is no post-filing cooling-off period in Irish divorce. But the description (metadata and template) says the 2-year separation 'must already be satisfied before or by the date the court grants the decree'. Section 5(1)(a) fixes the reference point at institution, not decree: 'at the date of the institution of the proceedings, the spouses have lived apart from one another for a period of, or periods amounting to, at least [two years during the previous three years]'. The living-apart requirement must therefore be satisfied when proceedings are ISSUED; two of the three years are measured backwards from the institution date. (Living apart can include living in the same dwelling if not living together as a couple in an intimate and committed relationship — s.5(1A), inserted by Family Law Act 2019 s.3(1)(b).)
waitingPeriod.correct: No mandatory post-filing waiting period; the spouses must have lived apart for at least 2 of the 3 years immediately preceding the DATE OF INSTITUTION OF THE PROCEEDINGS (Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996, s.5(1)(a) as amended), not merely by the date the decree is granted.

court.note: Courts Service: 'Most applications for divorce are made in the Circuit Court. In some situations where assets are valued over €3 million, an application can be made to the High Court. Divorce applications are not dealt with in the District Court.' The Circuit Court sitting in family matters is the Circuit Family Court (Judicial Separation and Family Law Reform Act 1989 s.31; FLDA 1996 s.38), so the template's 'CIRCUIT FAMILY COURT — [COUNTY]' with 'Record No.' matches practice (formal headings also carry 'AN CHÚIRT CHUARDA / THE CIRCUIT COURT, [X] Circuit'). The Family Courts Act 2024 (No. 48 of 2024, signed 13 Nov 2024) will create a Family Circuit Court, but the new family court divisions are not due to begin operating until about January 2027 (https://www.lawsociety.ie/gazette/top-stories/2026/april/first-family-courts-to-start-next-january/), so the current naming remains correct as of 2026-08-12.

The error is the amending pinpoint: both the metadata statute field and the template's RENDERED grounds text cite 'section 9 of the Family Law Act 2019'. The Family Law Act 2019 (No. 37 of 2019) has only 7 sections; the substitution of 'at least two years during the previous three years' in s.5(1)(a) was made by SECTION 3(1)(a) (s.3(1)(b) inserted the s.5(1A) living-apart definition). Section 5 of the 2019 Act is 'Definitions and application (Part 3)' — UK/Gibraltar divorce recognition; there is no section 9.
